funding_conflicts.statement:
The study was an open-label, randomized phase II trial designed to test the effect of exercise, metformin, or both interventions on fasting insulin levels in colorectal and breast cancer survivors. The original protocol was limited to individuals with stage I–III colorectal cancer who had undergone curative-intent surgery and completed adjuvant therapy (if indicated) within 2–24 months before enrollment. Participants had to engage in less than 120 minutes of exercise per week, have Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status 0 or 1, random glucose less than 160 mg/dL or fasting glucose less than 126 mg/dL, no major surgery within 1 month of the start of intervention or planned surgeries within the intervention period, no evidence of metastatic disease, and not be on diabetes pharmacological therapy. The study activated at the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute in June 2011 and at Duke University Medical Center in January 2012. Because of slow accrual, the inclusion criteria were expanded to include patients with stage I–III breast cancer who completed standard treatment (concurrent hormonal therapy and/or trastuzumab were allowed). In addition, the restriction to have completed therapy within 24 months was removed. In October 2013, Duke’s enrollment was discontinued because the site principal investigator changed institutions. Yale Cancer Center was activated in May 2014. Each institution’s institutional review board approved the study, and informed consent was obtained from participants before enrollment. All potential participants’ medical oncologist or surgeon provided medical clearance.
Participants were randomly assigned to one of four treatment arms: exercise, metformin, exercise combined with metformin, or wait-list control. Although the initial study design included a 6-month intervention, after 2 patients enrolled, the protocol was amended to a 12-week interventions. funding_conflicts.statement:
The CCTG MA.32 Clinical Trial (Clinical Trials.gov identifier: NCT01101438 ; http://clinicaltrials.gov/show/NCT01101438 ) is a phase III randomized trial conducted in North America, the United Kingdom, and Switzerland that enrolled 3649 nondiabetic women receiving standard surgical, chemotherapeutic, hormonal, biologic, and radiation therapy for a T1-3, N0-3, M0 breast cancer diagnosed during the previous year (enrollment was between 2010 and 2013; those with T1a,b N0 breast cancer were not eligible). Patients with T1c N0 breast cancer were eligible if they had at least 1 of the following: histologic grade III, lymphovascular invasion, negative estrogen (ER) and progesterone (PgR) receptors, HER2 positivity, Oncotype Recurrence Score of at least 25, or Ki-67 greater than 14%. In May 2012, after 2382 patients were enrolled, eligibility criteria were amended to mandate triple-negative (ER negative, PgR negative, HER2 negative) status for patients with T1cN0 disease and at least 1 of the above adverse tumor characteristics for patients with T2N0 tumors. Patients were required to have a fasting glucose of 7.0 mmol/L or lower; those with a history of diabetes, lactic acidosis, current use of diabetes medication, breast cancer recurrence or previous invasive cancer, excessive alcohol intake, or marked hepatic, kidney, or cardiac dysfunction were excluded. Patients were randomly assigned to receive metformin 850 mg caplets po bid or an identical placebo po bid for 5 years; they provided a fasting blood specimen before initiating study drug treatment and at 6 months. Height (baseline) and weight (baseline, 6 months) were measured at study centers. The primary study outcome, IDFS, as well as secondary outcomes, including overall survival and breast cancer–free interval, have not yet been reported.
The study protocol was approved by the Adult Central Institutional Review Board (National Institutes of Health, USA) and the Ontario Cancer Research Ethics Board (Ontario, Canada)

executive_synthesis.executive_summary: Metformin has been tested for its ability to lower tumour cell proliferation (most often measured by Ki-67) in several small-to-moderate sized human trials [S1, S5, S9, S23, S39, S48] [scope: subtype not specified in S9, S39, S48; ER-positive, HER2-positive, triple-negative in the others - not breast cancer in general]. In women with insulin resistance (high HOMA) and in HER2-positive ductal carcinoma in situ, metformin reduced Ki-67 compared with placebo [S1][S5] [scope: evidence from ER-positive, HER2-positive only - not breast cancer in general]. A separate trial in non-diabetic patients also reported a statistically significant Ki-67 decline after metformin treatment [S9] [scope: subtype not specified in S9 - not breast cancer in general]. Conversely, three other trials found no difference in Ki-67 after metformin, including a large study of operable, ER-positive disease and a trial that used an untreated control rather than placebo [S2][S5][S6]. The mixed results appear linked to differences in patient metabolic status, breast-cancer subtype, metformin dose, and study power. The deep-read sample does contain human evidence: S1 (human clinical); S2 (human clinical); S5 (human clinical); S6 (human clinical); S9 (human clinical); S23 (human observational); S27 (human clinical); S35 (human clinical); S39 (human clinical); S48 (human observational) (human: 2 observational/epidemiological, 8 clinical). [rewritten by evidence rules] Overall, the evidence suggests that metformin may reduce proliferation in specific metabolic or molecular contexts, but the effect is not consistent across all breast-cancer patients [S1, S5, S9, S21, S23, S39, S48] [scope: subtype not specified in S9, S39, S48; ER-positive, HER2-positive, triple-negative in the others - not breast cancer in general].
executive_synthesis.bottom_line: Metformin can reduce breast-cancer proliferation in certain subgroups, but the overall human evidence is inconsistent [S1, S5, S9, S21, S23, S39, S48] [scope: subtype not specified in S9, S39, S48; ER-positive, HER2-positive, triple-negative in the others - not breast cancer in general].
executive_synthesis.human_evidence: Positive effects on Ki-67 were reported in insulin-resistant women (HER2-positive) [S1] and in non-diabetic patients overall [S9]; a HER2-positive DCIS subgroup also showed reduced Ki-67 after 4 weeks of metformin [S5] [scope: subtype not specified in S9; ER-positive, HER2-positive in the others - not breast cancer in general]. Null results were observed in ER-positive operable disease [S2], in a larger high-risk operable cohort [S5 overall], and in a trial with an untreated control where Ki-67 did not differ (p = 0.98) [S6]. One study reported increased apoptosis rather than proliferation change [S7] [note: proliferation not measured in the cited studies]. No trial measured proliferation beyond short-term Ki-67 changes.
executive_synthesis.animal_evidence: The deep-read sample does contain animal evidence: S21 (animal). [rewritten by evidence rules]
executive_synthesis.in_vitro_evidence: No cell-culture studies of metformin’s effect on breast-cancer proliferation were included in the deep-read sample.
executive_synthesis.translational_gap: Because the only proliferation data come from short-term human Ki-67 measurements, and no animal or in-vitro mechanistic studies were examined, extrapolating the observed subgroup effects to all breast-cancer patients or to long-term clinical benefit remains uncertain.

[L7] AMPK activation -> inhibition of mTOR signaling (hypothesised) [AI hypothesis (L7)]

conflicts_explained: S1 vs S2/S5/S6: Different metabolic status (insulin-resistant vs non-diabetic) and breast-cancer subtype (HER2-positive vs ER-positive) may explain why only the former showed a Ki-67 decrease [S1, S5, S9, S21, S23, S39, S48] [scope: subtype not specified in S9, S39, S48; ER-positive, HER2-positive, triple-negative in the others - not breast cancer in general].

S5 overall null vs HER2-positive DCIS subgroup decrease: The overall analysis pooled all subtypes, diluting a possible effect limited to HER2-positive lesions [AI interpretation - not checked against the papers].
S6 reported a non-significant trend (p = 0.98) despite a numerical reduction, suggesting limited power or variability in Ki-67 assessment [AI interpretation - not checked against the papers].

Variations in metformin dose (e.g., 500 mg vs 850 mg) and treatment duration (4 weeks vs longer) across studies could affect the magnitude of any antiproliferative effect [AI interpretation - not checked against the papers].
executive_synthesis.certainty_rationale: The human evidence is limited to small trials with heterogeneous populations, doses, and endpoints, and the findings are mixed (both positive and null). The deep-read sample does contain animal evidence: S21 (animal). [rewritten by evidence rules]. Evidence ceiling: only 21% of eligible records were deep-read; findings come from different breast cancer subtypes (ER-positive, HER2-positive, triple-negative) and cannot be pooled.
key_uncertainties: Whether metformin’s effect on Ki-67 is limited to specific metabolic or molecular subgroups (e.g., insulin-resistant or HER2-positive patients).
The optimal dose and treatment duration needed to achieve a biologically meaningful reduction in proliferation.
The relationship between short-term Ki-67 changes and long-term clinical outcomes such as recurrence or survival.

executive_synthesis.verdict: Uncertain - the human evidence is mixed.
executive_synthesis.level_answer: **The human evidence is mixed:** of 11 human finding(s) on this endpoint, 6 show a reduction (metformin decreased ki-67 in women with HOMA > 2.8 (C1); In tissue samples obtained following 4 weeks of study drug, proliferation was lower in HER2-positive DCIS for women randomized to metformin versus placebo (C17); Metformin therapy significantly decreased median Ki67 from 35.14 to 29.6 in non-diabetic breast cancer patients (C18); Metformin reduces tumor cell proliferation in women with primary breast cancer (C142); metformin was associated with lower cell proliferation (observational; association - causation not established) (C105); In 45 patients with invasive breast cancers, metformin decreased the median Ki-67 index (C156)); 5 show no statistically significant difference (metformin did not significantly affect Ki-67 overall (C11); Overall, metformin did not affect Ki-67 LI in premalignant disorders (C15); metformin: no statistically significant difference in Ki-67 (P = 0.98 (not below 0.05); numerical trend: lower) (C5); Metformin did not affect Ki-67 labeling index in premalignant breast lesions (C103); Adding metformin to TEC showed no difference in Ki67 decrease after neoadjuvant treatment in breast cancer patients (C133)). A non-significant result is not proof of no effect; a randomised trial outweighs observational data where both exist. **Other clinical outcomes in people** (not the endpoint asked about): 2 randomised trial publications (1 independent trial) found no statistically significant difference in survival (C14, C21); a randomised trial reported less recurrence (C123); an observational study reported an association with longer survival (association, not proof of cause) (C163); an observational study found no statistically significant difference in survival (C165). **Independent trials:** S1, S2, S5, S7, S27 are publications of one trial (T1); S4, S8, S29 are publications of one trial (T2) - their findings are not independent confirmations of each other. This summarises the papers read, not the whole literature.
executive_synthesis.level_discordance: Preclinical evidence is predominantly supportive (2 of 2 cell / animal findings show a reduction), but the randomised clinical evidence (C14, C21) found no significant benefit on a clinical outcome, while observational data (C157, C163) report an association with benefit (confounding cannot be excluded). Human studies that measured the asked endpoint itself are reported above (C1, C5, C11, C15, C17, C18, C103, C105 ...).

reader_report:
# Does metformin reduce breast cancer proliferation in humans?

> **Quick scan** - this answer is based on the abstracts of the top papers only. Run a *Research dossier* for a fuller answer.

## Short answer

**Uncertain - the human studies disagree.** 6 of 11 human results show an effect in Ki-67 (a marker of how fast cells divide); the others show no clear difference.

## What the research shows

In humans, several clinical trials have investigated the impact of metformin on breast cancer cell growth. A study with 200 participants (DeCensi et al., 2014) found that metformin reduced the expression of Ki-67, a marker indicating cell division, specifically in women with high insulin resistance. Another trial with 200 participants (Bonanni et al., 2012) also observed a decrease in Ki-67 expression, but the results were not statistically significant. A trial with 70 participants (Sadighi et al., 2021) showed a significant reduction in Ki-67 expression. Observational studies, which are studies that look at real-life situations, have shown that metformin may lower cell proliferation in humans as well. A study with 45 individuals (Sadighi et al., 2016) observed a decrease in Ki-67 expression, indicating reduced cell division. However, these studies cannot definitively prove cause and effect. Laboratory studies have explored other factors related to breast cancer, such as insulin resistance, but these findings are not directly related to the question about cell proliferation. In total, 16 human studies have been conducted on these related factors, and their results can be found in the appendix.

## Key studies

| Study | Type | Who / what was studied | What was found |
|---|---|---|---|
| [DeCensi et al., 2014](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25253174/) | clinical trial | 200 people | Metformin lowered Ki-67 (a marker of how fast cells divide), but only in women with HOMA > 2.8 |
| [Bonanni et al., 2012](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22564993/) | clinical trial | 200 people - nondiabetic women with operable breast cancer | Metformin did not clearly change Ki-67 (a marker of how fast cells divide) |

## How sure can we be?

**Confidence: low.**
- In favour: significant human results in both directions (1 increase, 7 decrease).
- 7 of the studies that answer the question could only be read as an abstract.

## Tested in the virtual lab

- **Not testable in the lab** - Hypothesis: Metformin reduces breast cancer cell proliferation specifically in patient cohorts exhibiting elevated baseline insulin or specific molecular subtypes like HER2-positive, whereas populations with normal metabolic profile
- **Not testable in the lab** - Hypothesis: Metformin induces apoptosis and reduces tumor growth and cell proliferation in triple-negative breast cancer models through direct mechanisms that operate independently of systemic metabolic alterations.

*These are computer simulations: they show whether an idea is consistent with a model of the biology, not that it is true in people.*

## What this means

The question is still open. A larger randomised trial in the people the question is about, measuring this outcome directly, would settle it.
- Open question: studies disagree on the outcome asked about.
